The operator \(\vec P\) is just the spin‑\(1/2\) operator
\[
\vec P = \frac{\hbar}{2}\,\vec\sigma
\]
with Pauli matrices  

\[
\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

A direction \(\vec n\) that lies in the \(x\!-\!z\) plane can be written as  

\[
\vec n = (\sin\theta,\,0,\,\cos\theta),
\]
where \(\theta\) is the polar angle measured from the \(+z\) axis.

The component of \(\vec P\) along \(\vec n\) is  

\[
\vec P\!\cdot\!\vec n = \frac{\hbar}{2}\bigl(\sigma_x\sin\theta + \sigma_z\cos\theta\bigr)
 =\frac{\hbar}{2}
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos\theta & \sin\theta\\[2pt]
\sin\theta & -\cos\theta
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

We need the normalized eigenvector with eigenvalue \(+\hbar/2\).  
Setting up the eigenvalue equation  

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos\theta & \sin\theta\\[2pt]
\sin\theta & -\cos\theta
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}a\\ b\end{pmatrix}
= +1\begin{pmatrix}a\\ b\end{pmatrix},
\]

gives  

\[
\cos\theta\, a + \sin\theta\, b = a \;\Rightarrow\; (1-\cos\theta)a = \sin\theta\, b.
\]

Using the identities \(1-\cos\theta = 2\sin^2(\theta/2)\) and \(\sin\theta = 2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)\),

\[
2\sin^2(\theta/2)\, a = 2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)\, b
\;\Longrightarrow\;
a = \frac{\cos(\theta/2)}{\sin(\theta/2)}\, b.
\]

Choosing the normalization \(|a|^2+|b|^2=1\) and the simplest phase (real and positive) yields  

\[
b = \sin(\theta/2),\qquad a = \cos(\theta/2).
\]

Hence the normalized eigenvector corresponding to eigenvalue \(+\hbar/2\) is  

\[
|\,\uparrow_{\vec n}\,\rangle = 
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\\[4pt]
\sin\frac{\theta}{2}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Among the given choices, this matches option **(B)**.

**Answer: B**
